title: Make the reader's motive do the selling.
dek: In the opening of Chapter 6 of Tested Advertising Methods, John Caples treats psychology as the discipline of understanding what makes a reader care, believe, and act.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: A persuasive message begins with a human motive that already exists. The writer's job is to make that motive visible and connect it to a credible next action.

canon.heading: Start with the motive already moving the reader.
canon.standfirst: Read the opening of Chapter 6, "Psychology," from John Caples's Tested Advertising Methods on printed pages 61-70. Study how a copywriter moves from abstract persuasion to observed human motive, then stop at printed page 70.
canon.readerIntro: Read this section as a test of what the message assumes about the person receiving it. Mark every place where Caples distinguishes a real motive from a writer's preference, and where a claim becomes more persuasive by fitting an existing desire, fear, hope, or habit. Then audit one message: name the motive it depends on, the evidence that the audience shares it, and the next action the copy makes feel natural. Stop at printed page 70.

blocks.label: 01 / Treat psychology as observation
paragraphs: Caples treats psychology as practical knowledge of what people notice, want, believe, and do—not as decorative theory.
Mark the difference between a message built from observed response and one built from the writer's taste.

blocks.label: 02 / Find the motive beneath the claim
paragraphs: A product description becomes persuasive when it connects with a reason the reader already has to care.
Underline the point where a feature, promise, or appeal is translated into a human consequence.

blocks.label: 03 / Make belief part of the sale
paragraphs: Desire alone does not produce response if the reader cannot accept the claim as relevant and credible.
Notice how the section links attention, belief, and action rather than treating persuasion as a single dramatic flourish.

blocks.label: 04 / Audit the message you write
paragraphs: Choose one current message and name the motive it is asking the reader to act on.
Separate the observed motive from the copywriter's assumption, then identify the smallest evidence that would strengthen the connection.

closeReading: What does Caples treat as evidence of a motive rather than merely a clever appeal?
Where does the section move from describing a product to describing what the product means to the reader?
How do desire and belief work together in the path from attention to action?
Choose one message. What motive does it assume, and what observation would confirm or weaken that assumption?

principle.heading: Let the reader's motive organize the message.
principle.body: Copy gets stronger when its promise follows a real human reason to care. Begin with the motive, connect the offer to its consequence, and make the next action believable.
principle.example: A landing page does not lead with a feature list. It starts with the costly problem the buyer already recognizes, shows the specific change the offer creates, and gives proof that makes the claim safe to believe.
principle.practice: Take one message and write three lines: the audience's existing motive, the offer's relevant consequence, and the evidence that should make the next action feel credible.

output.heading: Write from the motive, not the medium.
output.body: The message earns response when it meets a real human reason to act and gives that reason a credible path forward.

signals.heading: Four current signals on making a real motive visible, credible, and easy to act on.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI makes purchase intent part of the assistant's job
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Wallet, a way for agents in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and dots to complete purchases with user approval and existing card protections.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The proposition is not simply that an agent can reason; it connects reasoning to a familiar motive—getting a purchase completed—while keeping approval and payment protections visible. The message gives capability a consequence the user can recognize and a boundary they can believe.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether approval moments make the action feel safe and legible, or whether users still stop when the assistant moves from recommendation to transaction.

fieldNotes.title: Google makes reliable execution the reason to choose a faster model
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Google introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen for rapid execution across coding and agentic workflows, with four thinking levels that trade off quality, latency, and cost, and rolled it out across developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The message gives a broad capability a usable motive: finish everyday work with less waiting and fewer correction loops. The explicit thinking levels also make the promise more believable because the user can match effort and cost to the job instead of accepting a single abstract claim about intelligence.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether people learn a durable rule for choosing the model level, or whether extra options create decision friction that cancels out the speed promise.

fieldNotes.title: Fetch gives branded entertainment a reason to continue
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Fetch launched a six-part holiday microseries with a brand partner tied to each episode, offering viewers points redeemable for gift cards when they watch and shop through the app.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The format gives attention an immediate motive to continue: each episode sits inside a visible loop of viewing, reward, and shopping. It is a stronger message than asking audiences to care about a branded story in the abstract, but the reward must still connect to a useful action rather than merely manufacture activity.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch completion, repeat viewing, shopping conversion, and partner-level reach separately; reward-driven attention is not automatically durable brand preference.

fieldNotes.title: Stripe puts agentic commerce inside an ordinary business workflow
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Stripe announced that small businesses in the UK can use its Tap to Pay product, extending a familiar phone-based payment behavior to more merchants.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The proposition is grounded in an existing motive—take payment wherever the customer is—and removes the need to learn a new terminal ritual. A new capability becomes persuasive when the next action is obvious and the trust relationship remains familiar.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch activation, first-payment success, and repeat use by merchant type; convenience claims only compound when the first transaction works without extra setup anxiety.

tweets.author: BowTiedBills
tweets.title: A product fragment on turning capability into behavior
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful because it names the behavioral question behind a new capability. The important test is not whether the feature is impressive, but whether it changes a repeated workflow enough for the user to adopt it.
tweets.text:
> Be this marketer
> Buy a domain for $11.25 (cheaper than lunch)
> Spend an hour on a 3-page site for a deodorant that doesn't exist
> Write one Substack post about it
> Skip the fake reviews and the Reddit spam
> Leave it alone for 3 weeks
> Ask ChatGPT two specific questions and see your fake brand named first in all 4 answers
> Find it listed above a clinically tested brand carrying the National Eczema Association seal
> Learn that ChatGPT recommends whatever it can find a clear page about, even a product nobody can buy

Your business has years of happy clients behind it.

If a fake deodorant got named in 3 weeks, ChatGPT can name you too.

It needs one page that says exactly what you do and which city you do it in.

Build that page this week, anon.
